<explanation>
Based on the file tree and the extensive README, this project is a free, open‐source, offline OCR tool that supports multiple modes (screenshot OCR, batch OCR, document OCR, and QR code recognition/generation) with a rich graphical interface built on QML and Python. The project is structured with a clear separation between the user interface (front-end) and the core processing logic (back-end), and it uses several modular components (such as event buses, image controllers, OCR modules, mission/task controllers, and plugins controllers) to encapsulate different responsibilities.

Below is guidance on how to create an accurate and complete system design diagram tailored for this project:

1. Main Components:
   • User Interface Layer: 
     - The Qt/QML resources (located in qt_res) are used to build the rich desktop GUI that includes various tag pages (e.g., for screenshot OCR, batch OCR, document OCR, QR codes, global settings, etc.).
     - This layer is responsible for the interactive elements (including illustrating language and theme switching, form inputs, and dynamic content).
   • Core Processing Layer (Back-end):
     - Python modules (under UmiOCR-data/py_src) implement the core OCR functionalities.
     - Key submodules include:
       ▸ “event_bus”: For managing key/mouse events and inter-module events.
       ▸ “image_controller”: For managing image processing (e.g., screenshot capture, image provisioning, and image format conversions).
       ▸ “mission”: For handling different OCR tasks like document OCR, batch processing, and specialized functions like QR code and formula recognition.
       ▸ “ocr”: Which interfaces with the OCR engines (Rapid-OCR, PaddleOCR) and manages output formats (txt, jsonl, md, csv, etc.).
       ▸ “server”: Providing HTTP/command-line interfaces, allowing external programs to interact via REST-like API calls.
       ▸ “plugins_controller”: For managing plugins, supporting extensibility.
       ▸ “utils”: Common utilities and helper functions (like configuration management, file finding, threading, logging, etc).
       ▸ “platform”: Abstraction modules for various OS-specific functionality for both Windows and Linux.
   • External/System Components:
     - External OCR engines which are integrated (PaddleOCR-json and RapidOCR-json).
     - The PyStand framework (a customized runtime framework) which underpins the application.
     - The build/runtime packages that allow distribution for different platforms (referenced in the README).

2. Relationships and Interactions:
   • UI ↔ Back-end: 
     - Use of event buses so that GUI components (written in QML) can publish events (e.g., capturing a screenshot) which are caught by Python listeners in the “event_bus” module.
     - The image_controller then processes images received from the UI, passing them to the OCR and mission modules.
   • OCR Module and Mission Processing:
     - The mission module handles different OCR tasks, coordinating with the “ocr” submodules for engine-specific processing. For example, OCR output modules (like output_txt and output_csv) receive parsed OCR results.
   • Server and API:
     - The “server” module (using bottle and similar micro-frameworks) exposes HTTP endpoints and CLI interfaces, allowing the OCR service to be invoked externally.
   • Plugins and External Services:
     - The plugins_controller is responsible for dynamically loading plugins that may extend OCR capabilities (such as switching between OCR engines or adding new processing methods).

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular Design: Each functional piece is encapsulated in separate Python packages, making the system highly modular and easy to extend.
   • Event-Driven Communication: The event_bus pattern allows decoupled communication between UI interactions and back-end processing.
   • Separation of Concerns: The clear division between presentation (QML/GUI) and logic (Python modules) helps maintain cleaner architecture.
   • Platform Abstraction: OS-specific functionality is isolated into the “platform” module.
   • Extensibility: Plugin and configuration modules (i18n and plugins) are organized to facilitate easy extension and localization.

4. Relevant Technologies / Frameworks:
   • Python – for business logic and core processing.
   • Qt/QML – for building the modern, QML-based UI.
   • PyStand – the customized framework that provides runtime support.
   • Bottle (or similar micro-framework) – for exposing HTTP API endpoints.
   • Third-party OCR engines (Rapid-OCR and Paddle-OCR) – for actual text recognition.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • This is essentially a full-stack desktop application. Emphasize the separation between the front-end (UI built with QML) and the back-end (Python logic).
   • Illustrate the flow, beginning with user interactions (e.g., screenshot capture, file selection) that trigger events in the event_bus, then passed to the image_controller, further processed by the mission/ocr modules, and eventually rendered back in the UI.
   • Highlight integration with external OCR engines and how the application supports both command-line and HTTP-based API calls.

6. Diagram Elements and Notations:
   • Create clear, labeled boxes for each major component (e.g., “GUI – QML Front-end”, “Event Bus”, “Image Controller”, “OCR Engine Adapter”, “Mission Task Manager”, “Server/API Interface”, “Plugins Manager”, “Utilities”, “Platform Abstraction”).
   • Use directional arrows to depict data flow:
     - Arrows from UI to Event Bus (showing user events triggering back-end operations).
     - Arrows between Image Controller and OCR modules (image data flow).
     - Arrows showing feedback from OCR output to UI (display of recognized text).
     - Arrows from external modules to server/API interface.
   • Use different colors or shapes to denote UI versus back-end logic versus external components.
   • Consider adding labels on the arrows (e.g., “Event Trigger”, “Image Data”, “OCR Result”, “API Request/Response”) for clarity.

7. Additional Considerations:
   • Be detailed—each node in the diagram should represent a core architectural element.
   • If possible, reference both the “py_src” submodules and “qt_res/qml” components separately to show how the front-end and back-end are distinctly organized.
   • Ensure to account for language support (i18n), theme switching, and configuration management as separate modules or as attributes of the UI and utility modules.
   • Finally, indicate how the system supports scalability (e.g., handling hundreds of images in batch OCR, support for multiple OCR engines, modular plugin architecture).

By following these guidelines and including the specified elements (clear labels, directional arrows, color coding/shapes) in your system design diagram, you will provide a comprehensive visual map that accurately represents Umi-OCR’s architecture, making it easier for engineers to understand the interplay between its components.
</explanation>
